rows.evidence: Q1: Sec. 2 - primary survey of 131 drip-adopter households in Pokharathok village (Palpa, Nepal) with unstructured interviews, random-spot observation over 3 weeks, focus groups and benefit-cost analysis. Q2: Sec. 3.2 - before drip only 3% of households produced vegetables and 72% of farmers ate no vegetables at meals; after intervention 100% of drip users consumed vegetables with meals; about 30% bought milking cows from vegetable income so milk products now in meals; Table 2 - majority agree drip changed daily vegetable intake; Sec. 4 concludes significant positive impact on family food and nutritional intake. Q4: Sec. 3.3/Table 5 - intermediate pathway measured: household vegetable production (kg), gross income ~US$67 per plot, women's access to vegetable income (Sec. 3.2: 92% had no income before). Q6: Sec. 2/3.2 - result reported across a village sample of 131 adopter households, i.e., community/village level rather than a single plot. Q7: Sec. 3.3 - states income generation is not possible unless a reliable, sustained output market exists; access to water is the key factor and market sustenance and credit access are crucial; Sec. 4 - benefits realised when technology offered within favourable institutional environment with facilitation by intervening agency. Q8: Sec. 4 - long-term sustainability of the livelihood is questionable; degree to which outside institutional support made the technology viable is not known; returns depend on market prices.
rows.notes: Dietary change evidence rests on recall-based survey and group discussions (self-report, no measured intake, no non-adopter control); qualitative discussion and survey are both respondent-report so not treated as independent methods. Single village, so no representativeness. No dispersion measures; only percentages and means. Q6 judged yes because effect is reported for a village-wide household sample, but it is an aggregation of household results rather than a scheme/district assessment.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sec. 2 - own survey of 131 adopter households, observation, focus groups and benefit-cost analysis. Q2: Sec. 3.3/Table 5 - average gross household income ~US$67 from the average 0.013 ha drip plot; NPV US$16.1, BCR 2.4, IRR 37.9%, payback 1.6 years, indicating strong financial viability; Sec. 3.2 - 92% of women had no income source before adoption and now have access to and control of income; Table 2 - 84% agree drip generates more income than other livelihood options; Sec. 3.4 - technology financially viable with potential for poverty reduction; Dalits reported gains. Q4: Table 1 and Sec. 3.3 - intermediate variables measured: labour days, kit cost (~US$13), production costs, vegetable output and revenue feeding the BCA. Q6: Sec. 2 - result reported for a village-level sample of 131 households, beyond a single plot. Q7: Sec. 3.3 - without a reliable, sustained output market income generation is not possible; water access is key and credit access crucial; Sec. 3.4 - lack of capital is the major adoption constraint; Sec. 4 - credit and institutional facilitation needed. Q8: Sec. 4 - long-term sustainability questionable, returns depend on market prices and number of adopters, impact of withdrawal of institutional support unknown.
rows.notes: The passage is about income and poverty reduction; the study's own BCA and survey address drip-kit income directly, though the 'social_cohesion' function label fits less well (study also reports self-help savings groups formed with vegetable income, Sec. 3.2). Perception survey and BCA both derive from the same household survey, so not counted as triangulation. The >50% income increase cited from Gurung (2000) is not the study's own result. No control group, single village, no dispersion statistics.

notes: Working Paper 87 (published 2005, cited as 2004). Tables and reference list in the supplied text are font-garbled; percentages and BCA values were taken from the readable body text. Single-village case study of adopters only, no comparison group.
